idiom_name: hand-kept brace layout (K&R or kernel style) with early-return guard clauses; clang-format or indent(1) as the enforcer
implementation_notes: C has no canonical formatter and no block-shape mechanism, so the rectangle is produced by hand - brace placement, one tab stop per nesting level, delimiters aligned with the statement that opened them - and only checked mechanically once the project pins a style file: clang-format with a committed .clang-format, or GNU indent with the classic '-kr -i8'. The depth rule is the real content of the pattern here: the kernel style document keeps 8-character tabs precisely so that over-nesting is visible and states that more than three levels of indentation means the program should be fixed, which is this pattern's own remedy (extract a function or return early). Keep the classic hand form where the style is already fixed by the project (kernel subsystems, libc-derived trees): matching the surrounding file beats introducing a new shape into it.
pitfalls: Tabs versus spaces: mixing them, or setting a tab width other than the project's, makes the rectangle a lie for every reader whose editor disagrees - commit to one, and turn off editors' indent-tabs-mode for space-styled trees.
clang-format rewrites whole regions at once and its version changes the output; adopt it as a single dedicated commit and pin the version, or layout churn will mix into behaviour diffs.

A brace-less single-statement body is idiomatic in several C styles but silently changes control flow when a second statement is added; the rectangle convention is the argument for bracing anything that may grow.
